clouddrop.summary: When Jamie announced the release of Constant Companions (Deluxe Edition), she revealed that the album was “missing a song,” dropped at the last minute “for reasons I’d rather not get into.” She described it as “one of the most ambitious things I’ve ever recorded, and my favorite song I’ve ever written.” As detailed in the June 2024 edition of the Bandcamp subscriber-exclusive Jamie P Jam Pack series of compilations, this song originally took the name “Magnasanti”, a nod to a viral Sim City experiment in which an attempt at creating a city with the highest-possible population careened into a totalitarian urban prison. The idea was kicked around in many different permutations, one of which became another deluxe edition-exclusive song, “Manifesto”. Eventually, “Magnasanti” was finished for the deluxe edition. As opposed to the other additions in the deluxe edition, which were placed after “Machine Love” in the track order, this particular song was retroactively slotted into its originally intended spot on the tracklist, rechristened “Clouddrop”. Clocking in at just under seven minutes, “Clouddrop” is Jamie’s first dip into progressive rock, spanning three distinct movements and being replete with call-backs to preceding songs on the album. It is the point at which all the album’s threads converge, and it’s on here that it all comes together at an explosively emotional climax. “Clouddrop” is the darkest entry on the album, and indeed one of the darkest in Jamie’s catalog as a whole. Both musically and lyrically heavy, the song candidly portrays Teto in the midst of a suicide attempt, careening down a road as the other parts of herself (represented by GUMI and ANRI) desperately try to talk her out of it; it’s left ambiguous whether the road imagery is literal or metaphorical. Starting off in a frantic rush of mania and despair, Teto indicates that she’s fallen to the lowest possible point in her life: former joys only bring shame, self-help has failed, and her overall perception of herself and her circumstances has made her conclude that there’s no longer any point to staying alive. Eventually, she starts to realize just what she’ll give up on, at which point things slow to an elegiac crawl. Teto imagines the person she loves the most contemplating suicide herself out of grief. It drags her deeper into her despair and self-loathing – at which point the voices of ANRI and GUMI almost scream into Teto’s head, bringing her back from the brink. Her pace picks up again as she proclaims with overflowing energy that she wants to fly. Following this, the song slowly winds down as GUMI gives a final verse that echoes the ending of “Cadmium Colors”, though painting it in a new hopeful light. Finally, Jamie steps up to the microphone and sings the song’s closing lines, building off of her description of Teto as “the vocal synth that feels the most like a stand-in for my own voice [and that] almost seems to bring out parts of myself that are a bit too honest.” Accordingly, Jamie’s contribution to the vocals emphasize thoughts and experiences alluded to in the final segment of the song’s Bandcamp description: “and the warmest, most grateful and loving thanks to the other me for facing down that cliffside that jagged, twisted cliffside on the darkest day of our entire life and having the strength to turn around, heart in hand and drive the fuck home”

machine-love.summary: Conceived as a tribute to “Song of the Eared Robot” by Nwp8861, the earliest surviving Kasane Teto song in existence, “Machine Love” is a piece of many layers. On the surface, it is an ode to a computer program falling in love with its human user, taking a common trope in popular media and spinning it in its own, euphoric direction. On a deeper level, it’s a tribute to Kasane Teto herself, extolling her communal origins as a 2chan-created parody of Hatsune Miku that rapidly took on a life of her own. On even deeper levels, it’s a song about Jamie’s view of art and about trans joy, two especially favored subjects in Jamie’s work. All the while, this myriad of meanings is connected by the same guiding thread: the desire to discover the truths that lay hiding within artifice (as Jamie so often phrases it) and the fundamental need to bridge gaps in order to achieve fulfillment. According to Jamie, “Machine Love” was written in its entirety shortly after the release of Kasane Teto’s first Synthesizer V release, which had generated widespread attention online for how lifelike her vocals sounded, with many longtime fans (and others knowledgeable about her history) considering it a fulfilment of the lifelong headcanon that Teto strived to be seen as a “real Vocaloid.” Describing it as “my love letter to the entire world of unbridled creativity and artistry surrounding vocal synths filtered through one sentimental little song,” the track was specifically inspired by a SynthV cover of “Song of the Eared Robot” – as Jamie considered the original a personal favorite for years, the decision to homage it became inevitable. The piece was then recorded for the 2024 compilation album DAEMON/DOLL (released to commemorate the SynthV version of Teto’s first anniversary) before being remixed for inclusion on Constant Companions. The decision to put it on the latter was explained as follows: “There isn’t really a definitive answer to the specific question ‘Baby, do you know what you wanna hear?’, but [“Machine Love] evokes a theme running through the entire album - wanting something, knowing that you want something, and simply needing to find the courage to do it or say it or be it. ‘My Darling, My Companion’ is in many ways a declaration of intent, an acceptance of what needs to happen, but ‘Machine Love’, to me, is that action being done. The words being said!” Musically, “Machine Love” is a soaring rush of elation that both blazes like an inferno and quenches like an overflowing font. Prominently quoting “Song of the Eared Robot”, its anthemic approach fully conveys the multifaceted joy that inspired its creation. This approach and its connection to the lyrical themes are complimented by its elaborate music video, the first in Jamie’s career, which acts as a further love letter to Teto’s history and role in internet culture, referencing past songs and fan content (including the entire rest of the tracklist on DAEMON/DOLL) while emphasizing Teto’s desire to bridge the gap between the real and virtual worlds. Self-shot and supported by her friends and Twitter mutuals, Jamie affectionately described the final product as “scrappy, DIY bullshit,” being as sleek as it is palpably autodidactic. In that regard, both the song and video act as a firm embodiment of Teto’s past, present, and possible future.
